title: Git Ignore Files: 3 Ways to Exclude Files from Git
summary: Guide explaining Git's three ignore mechanisms: .gitignore for shared patterns, .git/info/exclude for personal project files, and global excludes for editor and OS junk. Each serves different audiences and keeps repository ignore rules clean.
content:
Most developers know one way to keep a file out of Git: add it to .gitignore. That works until you need to ignore something that is only yours, like an editor folder or a scratch notes file, and you do not want to commit a line about it to a shared repository. Git actually has three places for ignore rules, each for a different audience. Picking the right one keeps your project's .gitignore clean and stops your personal clutter from leaking into every pull request. I ran every command below on Git 2.43.0.



Method
Where it lives
Shared with team?
Applies to
Use it for




.gitignore
Inside the repo (committed)
Yes
That repo (and subfolders)
Build output, dependencies, secrets: things nobody should commit


.git/info/exclude
Inside the repo's .git folder
No
That repo only
Your personal files in one project


Global excludes file
Your home directory
No
Every repo on your machine
Editor and OS junk



That split matches how the official gitignore documentation describes them: patterns that "all developers will want to ignore" belong in .gitignore, patterns "specific to a particular repository but which do not need to be shared" belong in info/exclude, and patterns a user wants ignored "in all situations", such as editor backup files, belong in the file named by core.excludesFile.
Create a file called .gitignore in the repository root and commit it. A small example for a Laravel project:
.env
/vendor/
/node_modules/
/public/build/
*.log

In my test repo, with .env, build/ and *.log listed, git status stopped showing all three, and ordinary source files were untouched. You can check which rule matched a file with git check-ignore -v:
$ git check-ignore -v .env storage/logs/app.log build/out.js
.gitignore:1:.env   .env
.gitignore:3:*.log  storage/logs/app.log
.gitignore:2:build/ build/out.js

The output is file:line:pattern, then the path. A file that is not ignored prints nothing and the command exits with status 1, which makes it easy to use in scripts. A .gitignore in

title: Building a $0, no-backend portfolio backtester and the data-licensing rabbit hole
summary: Developer built BacktestCard, a zero-dependency static-site backtester for Indian investors using plain JavaScript. Navigated data licensing restrictions from Yahoo, Stooq, and FRED; implements portfolio state in URL hash with 200-line engine and 108 KB monthly data refresh.
content:
I built BacktestCard, a static-site backtester for Indian investors who measure in USD. It has no framework, no backend and no dependencies. Three things were more interesting than I expected.
Yahoo, Stooq and NSE all forbid redistribution.
FRED was the surprise. Its ToS bars storing or caching FRED content, even for public-domain series.
So the build script fetches from the publishers themselves:


Federal Reserve DDP for H.10 and H.15
BLS flat files
the OECD SDMX API
the World Bank Pink Sheet (CC BY 4.0)
The result is a 108 KB JSON file, refreshed monthly by a GitHub Action.
Licensed indices such as NIFTY come only through a user CSV upload. It's parsed with FileReader and never sent anywhere.
The engine is about 200 lines of plain JS. The tests include a separate pandas implementation that must match every statistic to 1e-9. On day one it disagreed on bond returns.
Bond returns are modelled from yields. Each month you buy a 10-year par bond and reprice it at the new yield. I had added coupon/12 on top of a dirty price that already included accrued interest, which added 1.4%/yr of phantom return to a 60/40 mix. The fix uses a closed form:
// remaining flows at j/2 - 1/12 years => dirty = (1+y/2)^(1/6) * P_20(y)
return Math.pow(1 + y / 2, 1 / 6) * price20 - 1;

The whole portfolio state is in the hash, e.g. #p=us_eq:60,in_eq:40&s=2000-01&c=USD.
It's whitelisted on decode, so __proto__:5 gets dropped.
The share card is a 1200×630 canvas exported with toDataURL.
?embed=1 gives a compact iframe with a badge, which is the growth loop.
Code (MIT): https://github.com/Nidhi-bhai/backtestcard. It's educational only, not investment advice.

title: Six Open-Source Projects from VIDRAFT, Now on GitHub
summary: VIDRAFT releases six open-source projects on GitHub including ONGRID for GraphRAG with confidence scoring, FINAL Bench for model metacognition testing, quantum simulation harness, POCKET for CPU-only model inference, and ZTC for zero-token confidence detection.
content:
We keep most of our work on Hugging Face, but code belongs where developers already look for it. So the open parts of what we build now live on GitHub at github.com/final-bench. Here are six projects, what each one does, and where to start.
Most GraphRAG tools retrieve and generate. ONGRID adds the step that usually goes missing: deciding whether the answer can be trusted.
Drop in documents and ONGRID builds a 3D ontology graph of typed entities and relations. Ask a question and an LLM answers from facts in that graph. Then a confidence judge checks the answer without generating any tokens.
Repository: final-bench/ongrid
Accuracy benchmarks ask whether the final answer is right. FINAL Bench asks a different question: can a model detect its own error, admit it, and fix it?
It covers functional metacognition across 100 tasks in 15 domains, from mathematics and medicine to ethics and economics. The paper is on arXiv and the dataset is on Hugging Face.
Repository: final-bench/leaderboard
A leaderboard is only as trustworthy as its scoring code, so we published the scoring code.
The harness holds reproducible scoring and frozen test problems for the Open Quantum Challenge: quantum simulation tasks and surface-code decoder scoring, reported as logical error rate with 95% Wilson intervals. Anyone can run it and get the same numbers the leaderboard shows. Contestants keep their own methods to themselves.
Repository: final-bench/quantum-bench-harness
POCKET is a family of models quantized to run locally on a laptop CPU, with no GPU and no network connection.
The repository is the model index plus run recipes. The GGUF weights are on Hugging Face, where the POCKET builds have been downloaded more than two million times in total.
Repository: final-bench/pocket
ZTC (Zero-Token Confidence) reads a question and an answer written by any model and returns whether the answer can be trusted. It does this in one forward pass, without generating text.
It comes in 4B, 9B and 27B sizes,

title: Express Node.js Passwordless Phone Login — Auditing SMS OTP for Property Receipts
summary: Compliance-focused guide on implementing SMS OTP passwordless authentication. Emphasizes backend-controlled policy enforcement, comprehensive audit logging, and separating delivery success from actual verification to handle resends and lockouts safely.
content:
Compliance evidence is the deciding constraint in this design, not the SMS vendor. Short answer: keep passwordless phone challenge counters, expiry, resend eligibility, and lockout decisions in the backend database; after a property payment settles, attach the resulting access evidence to the receipt-delivery record. Use a hosted SMS OTP operation for delivery, but do not delegate policy to a button timer or assume that a successful provider request proves the right person received anything.
The useful artifact is a compact chain of decisions. It should answer who requested access, which policy version ran, why a resend was allowed or denied, whether verification consumed the challenge, and which communication decision followed settlement. This approach also contains cost: checking suppression before a send avoids repeatedly targeting a blocked number, while limits by phone, IP, and device make automated SMS spending harder to trigger.
A property manager does not need a transcript of every internal function call. They need enough durable data to reconstruct the decision without retaining the plaintext OTP. For each challenge, store an opaque challenge ID, a normalized phone reference, hashed code material, creation and expiry timestamps, failed verification count, send count, next-send timestamp, state, and policy version. Keep the IP and device signals required by the abuse policy under an explicit retention rule.
Four events are enough for the main trail: initial send, resend decision, verification decision, and lockout. Each event records a timestamp, outcome, reason code, challenge ID, and correlation ID. A denied resend belongs in the trail too. It shows that the server applied its cooldown rather than silently losing a request.
The browser's countdown is decoration. The database clock and an atomic update decide whether the next send is legal. Likewise, a resend must not reset failed verification attempts. Otherwise an attacker gets a fresh attempt budget by a

title: We audited 193 pages with our open-source GEO MCP. Here is what it found.
summary: WebDecoy built GEOMCP, an open-source MCP server for technical SEO audits, and ran it against 193 production URLs. Found 11 accessibility and structure issues; all warnings cleared after fixes deployed, validating the audit approach.
content:
We built GEOMCP, a free MIT-licensed MCP server for technical GEO and SEO checks. I’m on the WebDecoy team.
Then we ran it against all 193 URLs in our production sitemap through a real SDK client and stdio MCP server.
Five articles had unnamed checkboxes generated from Markdown task lists.
The glossary and bot report skipped a heading level.
Our Features page linked to AI Analytics with the label “Learn More.”
Three standalone pages had no contextual same-origin links in their main content.
We fixed the issues, deployed the changes, and ran the same MCP on those pages. All 11 original warnings cleared.
The run also found a bug in our comparison tool: it classified unchanged unknown results as coverage changes. We fixed that and added a regression test.
182 pages initially scored 100 on the basic checklist. That does not establish AI citations, perfect accessibility, good Core Web Vitals, or higher conversion. The evidence behind each check is more useful than treating the score as a forecast.
GEOMCP has five read-only tools: audit a URL, audit supplied HTML offline, inspect robots policies, inspect a sitemap, and compare reports. No API key is required. It inspects server-delivered HTML and does not run page scripts.
See the real before/after results, the demo, and installation instructions.
Source and MIT license. Feedback and reproducible issues are welcome.
This write-up was prepared with AI assistance from recorded test output and reviewed against the implementation.

title: Your Compose Screen Is Gone. Why Is Your Flow Still Running?
summary: Explains Android Compose lifecycle management for coroutine cancellation. Shows how lifecycle-aware collection using collectAsStateWithLifecycle prevents unnecessary background work after screen dismissal while maintaining proper task completion on navigation.
content:
Press Home on an Android app. The screen disappears, but that doesn't automatically mean every coroutine feeding it has stopped.
For a search screen, live dashboard, or AI response view, this distinction matters. A UI collector and the producer behind it have separate lifetimes. Reviewing only one can leave unnecessary work running—or stop work that the product actually needs to finish.
Here's a small pattern worth understanding before adding more architecture to a Compose screen.
For an Android Compose route backed by a ViewModel, use lifecycle-aware collection:
import androidx.compose.runtime.Composable
import androidx.compose.runtime.getValue
import androidx.lifecycle.compose.collectAsStateWithLifecycle

@Composable
fun FeedRoute(viewModel: FeedViewModel) {
    val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    FeedScreen(state)
}

FeedScreen is your rendering composable; FeedViewModel is supplied by your app's normal ViewModel creation mechanism. Add androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-runtime-compose using a version aligned with your project's Lifecycle dependencies.
By default, collection runs when the lifecycle is at least STARTED. It stops below that state and starts again when the lifecycle becomes active. This is different from ordinary collectAsState(), whose collection follows the composition rather than applying this lifecycle threshold. See the Android Compose state guide.
That fixes the consumer side. Now look upstream.
Here is an integration sketch for a repository that observes feed items. It assumes a cold Flow whose observation work is cancelled when its collector is cancelled. Adapt the model and repository to your app.

import androidx.lifecycle.viewModelScope
import kotlinx.coroutines.CancellationException
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.SharingStarted
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.StateFlow
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.catch

content:
As the current console cycle reaches its mid-generation peak with the PlayStation 5 Pro, industry attention has shifted toward Sony Interactive Entertainment's next major hardware milestone: the PlayStation 6 (PS6). Verified supply chain reports and silicon foundry contracts confirm that Sony has extended its multi-decade design partnership with AMD, selecting custom Zen 6 CPU cores and next-generation RDNA 5 (UDNA) graphics architecture to drive its tenth-generation console. This technical architecture analysis breaks down the expected hardware specifications, dedicated neural processing silicon for PSSR 2.0, memory bandwidth targets, and projected market deployment windows.
Sony’s choice to remain with AMD for the PlayStation 6 was driven by two engineering priorities: software compatibility across generations and cost-effective semi-custom manufacturing. While Intel aggressively bid for the contract during early packaging negotiations, transitioning to x86/Intel Xe graphics architectures would have fractured the backward-compatibility pipeline that allows PS4 and PS5 titles to execute without emulation layers.
The heart of the PS6 is an AMD Accelerated Processing Unit (APU) manufactured on TSMC's 3nm (N3P/N3X) process node. The CPU cluster features 8 to 12 high-performance Zen 6 cores built with hybrid execution paths, delivering dramatic IPC gains over the Zen 2 cores inside the baseline PS5. title: AI Call Automation Needs an Execution Ledger, Not Just a Conversation Flow
summary: Proposes execution ledger design pattern for AI calling systems to track authorization, attempted actions, outcomes, and reconciliation independently of conversational quality. Addresses operational safety by making uncertain behavior visible and containing failure blast radius.
content:
AI Call Automation Needs an Execution Ledger, Not Just a Conversation Flow


An AI calling system can sound natural and still be operationally unsafe. The hardest failures are rarely bad greetings or awkward pauses. They are uncertain outcomes: the provider accepted a request but the application timed out; a retry launches a second call; a transfer succeeds but the workflow records failure; a customer revokes consent while a campaign queue is already populated; a transcript says an appointment was booked while the calendar write never committed.
The useful design question is therefore not “Can the agent conduct this conversation?” It is: Can the business prove what was authorized, attempted, heard, changed, and reconciled for every call?
This guide turns AI call automation into an execution-control problem. The core artifact is a call execution ledger: an append-only record that binds purpose, consent, identity, policy, provider events, conversation outcomes, tool effects, human handoffs, and final reconciliation to one stable call intent. The ledger does not make a model accurate by itself. It makes uncertain behavior visible, limits the blast radius of mistakes, and gives operators a safe way to resume after partial failure.
The starting use case comes from this AI call automation field guide. The adaptation here takes a different angle: how to design the state machine and evidence path that must surround inbound and outbound calls before the system receives authority to act.
Voice is only the interface. The risk lives in the effects behind it. A call can create, change, or disclose something consequential: an appointment, a cancellation, a payment promise, an address, a support entitlement, a lead status, a marketing preference, a service interruption, or a transfer to a licensed professional.
Start by classifying every intended effect, not by listing conversational intents.

title: 견적 변경 알림의 상태 설계: sent를 applied로 쓰지 않기
summary: Korean guide on separating notification delivery states from business application states. Explains how to track quote change proposals with independent identifiers, preventing duplicate applications and ensuring proper workflow progression only after confirmed approval.
content:
견적 변경 메일을 자동화할 때 알림 성공을 업무 적용 완료로 기록하면 상태가 어긋납니다. 메일 발송 처리, 고객 의견, 조직의 승인 절차, 실제 적용은 서로 다른 사건이기 때문입니다.
아래는 특정 제품의 구현 설명이 아닌, 작은 업무 도구를 설계할 때 사용할 수 있는 예시입니다.
같은 변경안이 재전송되더라도 업무상 변경이 하나 더 생긴 것은 아닙니다. 변경 제안에는 고유 식별자를 두고 문서 버전, 비교 기준, 전달 시도를 따로 연결합니다.
{
  "change_id": "example-change-001",
  "baseline_version": "example-v1",
  "proposal_version": "example-v2",
  "workflow_status": "awaiting_review",
  "delivery_status": "sent",
  "review_evidence_ref": null,
  "applied_version": null
}

값은 모두 설명용입니다. 실제 도구에서는 조직의 데이터 분류·보관 기준에 맞춰 식별자를 사용하고 고객 정보나 견적 내용을 불필요한 로그에 복사하지 않습니다.
delivery_status=sent는 적용 조건이 아닙니다. 고객 확인과 내부 승인 방식에 맞는 근거가 확보돼야 다음 업무 단계로 전환할 수 있습니다. 열람 신호나 일정 시간의 경과만으로 applied_version을 채우지 않습니다.
또한 답변이 변경 범위에만 해당하고 일정에는 해당하지 않을 수 있습니다. 어떤 항목이 확인됐는지와 남은 질문을 분리해 기록해야 합니다.
변경 알림 템플릿에는 다음 세 부분을 둡니다.
기존 기준: 문서 버전과 실제 확인 상태
변경 제안: 작업 범위·비용·일정의 차이
다음 행동: 확인받을 항목과 적용 전후의 작업
요약을 생성하는 도구를 붙이더라도 미확정 금액이나 날짜를 채워 넣게 해서는 안 됩니다. 확인하지 못한 값은 명시적으로 비워 두고 검토 대상으로 보냅니다.
같은 알림을 재시도해도 변경안이 중복 생성되지 않는가?
발송 실패가 고객 거절로 저장되지 않는가?
범위만 확인한 답변을 전체 조건 확인으로 확대하지 않는가?
이전 변경안에 온 답변이 새 변경안을 적용하지 않는가?
적용 근거와 문서 버전이 어긋나면 사람이 확인할 수 있는가?
알림의 성공과 업무의 완료를 나누면 재시도와 사람 검토의 위치가 선명해집니다. 오피셜메일의 사업용 메일 안내도 함께 살펴보세요. 여러분의 도구에서는 고객 확인 근거와 적용 버전을 어떻게 연결하고 있나요?

title: PwnEscape: Guest-to-Host KVM Escape and Host Memory Leak via Linux Checksum Processing (CVE-2026-99999)
summary: Details CVE-2026-99999, a critical Linux kernel vulnerability allowing guest-to-host KVM escape through checksum metadata manipulation. CVSS 9.3 severity with reported memory leaks and host code execution confirmed in Vercel sandbox and research environments.
content:
1. Basic Information




Article Name: PwnEscape: Guest-to-Host KVM Escape (CVE-2026-99999)
Source: pwn.ai / PWNAI Research, Paulos Yibelo
Publication Date: October 15, 2026 (Estimated based on the article record creation date. The official publication date and time are not set.)
Updated Date: October 18, 2026, 11:20 JST (Original metadata)
Source URL: pwn.ai: PwnEscape


Related Information Sources: Linux CNA: CVE-2026-99999 Official Record, Linux Fix Commit 6785011f8b16, Vercel: Findings from the 1 Million Dollar Vercel Sandbox Challenge, Red Hat: CVE-2026-99999, Amazon Linux: CVE-2026-99999, Linux Kernel Documentation: Checksum Offloads, MITRE ATT&CK: Escape to Host


Related Malware / Attack Groups: None publicly disclosed
Related CVE: CVE-2026-99999
Related Products: Linux kernel IPv4 processing, virtio-net / TUN/TAP, KVM, Firecracker, Vercel Sandbox
Severity: Critical
The Linux CNA rated CVSS v3.1 at 9.3. The impact crosses the isolation boundary between the guest and the host, with production memory leaks and host code execution in researcher-owned environments reported. Red Hat assigned a score of 8.8; these scores come from different rating authorities.
A Linux flaw allows guest-provided checksum metadata to overwrite validated IPv4 headers. Production memory leaks and host code execution in a research environment have been reported, requiring remediation on the host kernel side.
The following are sequential phases described by pwn.ai. Additional memory manipulation is required to progress from the first half (memory leak) to the second half (host execution). This does not mean the entire attack can be reproduced using only the first part of the disclosure.



Phase
Verified Environment
Key Technical Actions
Confirmed Impact Scope




Phase 1
Vercel production sandbox and researcher-owned environments
